title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 145 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān ends
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 713–716 (Night 145, continuing directly from nights-144), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 145 brings the long tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān to its end. Nuzhat al-Zamān kills the Bedouin who kidnapped her; King Rūmzān beheads the black slave al-Ghaḍbān, who murdered his mother Abrīza; Kān Mā Kān kills the camel-driver who abandoned his sick father Ḍawʾ al-Makān on a dung-heap. Rūmzān lures the old woman Shawāhī, Dhāt al-Dawāhī, to Baghdad with a letter, the kings meet her dressed as Franks and seize her, and she is paraded and crucified at the city gate. The kings have the scribes set the story down, and Shahriyār asks Shahrazād for tales of birds. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu wa-al-arbaʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth-and-forty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and forty-fifth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا سَمِعَتْ مِنَ الْبَدَوِىِّ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ تَبَدَّلَ الضِّيَاءُ فِي عَيْنِهَا بِالظَّلَامِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Nuzhata al-Zamāni lammā samiʿat mina al-badawiyyi hādhā al-kalāma tabaddala al-ḍiyāʾu fī ʿaynihā bi-al-ẓalāmi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Nuzhat al-Zamān, when she heard from the Bedouin this speech, the radiance in her eye was-exchanged for the darkness.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Nuzhat al-Zamān heard these words from the Bedouin, the light in her eyes turned to darkness.
sentences.n: The print runs al-saʿīd into anna as one word, السعيدان; the spacing is kept and the join is pointed as al-saʿīdu anna. The new night opens by repeating the line on which the last one closed, with ḍiyāʾ, “radiance”, where Night 144 had nūr, “light”; kalām and ẓalām still rhyme. Nuzhat al-Zamān is set at the head of the clause and the sentence then turns to what happened to the light in her eyes. The print writes al-badawī with final ى.

sentences.t: وَقَامَتْ جَرَّدَتِ السَّيْفَ وَضَرَبَتْ بِهِ الْبَدَوِىَّ حَمَّادًا عَلَى عَاتِقِهِ فَأَطْلَعَتْهُ مِنْ عَلَائِقِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāmat jarradati al-sayfa wa-ḍarabat bihi al-badawiyya Ḥammādan ʿalā ʿātiqihi fa-aṭlaʿathu min ʿalāʾiqihi
sentences.l: And she rose, bared the sword, and struck with it the Bedouin Ḥammād on his shoulder, and made-it-come-out from his ties.
sentences.i: She rose, drew the sword, and struck Ḥammād the Bedouin on the shoulder, so that the blade came out through his vitals.
sentences.n: qāmat jarradat, “she rose, she bared”: two verbs side by side without “and”, a spoken pattern in which the first marks the start of the action. jarrada al-sayf, “to strip the sword”, to draw it. fa-aṭlaʿathu min ʿalāʾiqihi, literally “and she made it come out from his attachments”, is a stock rhyming phrase for a blow that cleaves right through (ʿātiqihi / ʿalāʾiqihi). ʿalāʾiq, “ties, things that hang together”, is taken to mean the sinews and cords that hold the body together, and the -hu most likely refers to the sword; the formula is loose and its exact sense uncertain. The hamza in علائقه is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْحَاضِرُونَ لِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ اسْتَعْجَلْتِ عَلَى قَتْلِهِ فَقَالَتِ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي فَسَحَ فِي أَجَلِي حَتَّى أَخَذْتُ ثَأْرِي بِيَدِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-ḥāḍirūna li-ayyi shayʾin istaʿjalti ʿalā qatlihi fa-qālati al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī fasaḥa fī ajalī ḥattā akhadhtu thaʾrī bi-yadī
sentences.l: And those-present said to her: For what thing did-you-hasten over his killing? And she said: Praise (be) to God, who made-room in my term until I took my blood-revenge with my hand.
sentences.i: Those present said to her, “Why were you so quick to kill him?” She said, “Praise be to God, who lengthened my days until I could take my vengeance with my own hand.”
sentences.n: The shadda in لايّ is the print's. istaʿjala ʿalā, “to be in a hurry over”. fasaḥa fī al-ajal, “to give room in the term”: ajal is the span of life God appoints to each person. thaʾr, “blood-revenge”. Ḥammād is the Bedouin who, by his own account in the last night, kidnapped her from Jerusalem and sold her.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا أَمَرَتِ الْعَبِيدَأَنْ يَجُرُّوهُ مِنْ رِجْلَيْهِ وَيَرْمُوهُ لِلْكِلَابِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā amarati al-ʿabīda an yajurrūhu min rijlayhi wa-yarmūhu li-al-kilābi
sentences.l: Then indeed she commanded the slaves that they drag-him by his two-feet and throw-him to the dogs.
sentences.i: Then she ordered the slaves to drag him off by the feet and throw him to the dogs.
sentences.n: The print runs al-ʿabīd into an as one word, العبيدان; the spacing is kept and the join is pointed as al-ʿabīda an. thumma innahā, “then she”, literally “then indeed she”, a narrator's filler. After an the verbs are subjunctive, yajurrūhu and yarmūhu, without the final -n. The shadda in يجرّوه is the print's.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَقْبَلُوا عَلَى الِاثْنَيْنِ الْبَاقِيَيْنِ مِنَ الثَّلٰثَةِ وَكَانَ أَحَدُهُمَا عَبْدًا أَسْوَدَ فَقَالُوا لَهُ مَا اسْمُكَ أَنْتَ فَاصْدُقْنَا فِي حَدِيثِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika aqbalū ʿalā al-ithnayni al-bāqiyayni mina al-thalāthati wa-kāna aḥaduhumā ʿabdan aswada fa-qālū lahu mā ismuka anta fa-uṣduqnā fī ḥadīthika
sentences.l: And after that they turned to the two remaining of the three, and one-of-them was a black slave; and they said to him: What (is) your name, you? And be-truthful-with-us in your telling.
sentences.i: After that they turned to the two who were left of the three. One of them was a black slave, and they said to him, “What is your name? And tell us your story truthfully.”
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, “to turn to, attend to”. mā ismuka anta, “what is your name, you?”, with the pronoun added at the end for emphasis, as in speech. ṣadaqa, “to speak truly to”, takes the hearer as its direct object: fa-uṣduqnā, “so be truthful with us”. The dagger alif in الثلٰثة is the print's: thalātha written without its long alif.

sentences.t: قَالَ أَنَا اسْمِي الْغَضْبَانُ وَأَخْبَرَهُمْ بِمَا وَقَعَ لَهُ مَعَ الْمَلِكَةِ أَبْرِيزَةَ بِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ حَرْدُوبَ مَلِكِ الرُّومِ وَكَيْفَ قَتَلَهَا وَهَرَبَ
sentences.tr: qāla anā ismī al-Ghaḍbānu wa-akhbarahum bi-mā waqaʿa lahu maʿa al-malikati Abrīzata binti al-maliki Ḥardūba maliki al-Rūmi wa-kayfa qatalahā wa-haraba
sentences.l: He said: I, my name (is) al-Ghaḍbān. And he told them of what befell him with Queen Abrīza, daughter of King Ḥardūb, king of the Rūm, and how he killed her and fled.
sentences.i: He said, “My name is al-Ghaḍbān,” and he told them all that had passed between him and Queen Abrīza, daughter of King Ḥardūb, king of the Rūm: how he had killed her and fled.
sentences.n: The print has حرودب, a misprint for حردوب, corrected here. anā ismī, “I, my name is”: the speaker set first and taken up again by the pronoun. The narrator does not retell the story; the nurse Marjāna told it in full in Night 143.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يُتِمَّ الْعَبْدُ كَلَامَهُ حَتَّى رَمَى الْمَلِكُ رُومْزَانُ رَقَبَتَهُ بِالْحُسَامِ وَقَالَ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي أَحْيَانِي وَأَخَذْتُ ثَأْرَ أُمِّي بِيَدِي وَأَخْبَرَهُمْ أَنَّ دَايَتَهُ مَرْجَانَةَ حَكَتْ لَهُ عَنْ هَذَا الْعَبْدِ الَّذِي اسْمُهُ الْغَضْبَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yutimma al-ʿabdu kalāmahu ḥattā ramā al-maliku Rūmzānu raqabatahu bi-al-ḥusāmi wa-qāla al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī aḥyānī wa-akhadhtu thaʾra ummī bi-yadī wa-akhbarahum anna dāyatahu Marjānata ḥakat lahu ʿan hādhā al-ʿabdi alladhī ismuhu al-Ghaḍbānu
sentences.l: And the slave had not completed his speech before King Rūmzān threw-off his neck with the sharp-sword, and said: Praise (be) to God who kept-me-alive, and I-have-taken the blood-revenge of my mother with my hand. And he told them that his nurse Marjāna had told him about this slave whose name (is) al-Ghaḍbān.
sentences.i: The slave had not finished speaking when King Rūmzān struck off his head with the sword and said, “Praise be to God, who has let me live to avenge my mother with my own hand.” And he told them that his nurse Marjāna had told him about this slave called al-Ghaḍbān.
sentences.n: lam … ḥattā, “he had not … when”: the second act cuts the first short. ramā raqabatahu, “he threw (off) his neck”, he beheaded him. ḥusām, “a keen sword”, a poetic word. aḥyānī wa-akhadhtu, “who kept me alive, and I have taken”: the second clause stands loosely beside the first, where the sense is “so that I have taken”. Rūmzān is Abrīza's son by King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The shadda in امّي is the print's. dāya, “nurse”, a word of Persian origin.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَقْبَلُوا عَلَى الثَّالِثِ وَكَانَ هُوَ الْجَمَّالَ الَّذِي اكْتَرَوْهُ أَهْلُ بَيْتِ الْمَقْدِسِ إِلَى حَمْلِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ وَتَوْصِيلِهِ إِلَى الْمَارَسْتَانِ الَّذِي فِي دِمَشْقِ الشَّامِ فَذَهَبَ بِهِ وَأَلْقَاهُ فِى الْمُسْتَوْقَدِ وَذَهَبَ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika aqbalū ʿalā al-thālithi wa-kāna huwa al-jammāla alladhī iktarawhu ahlu Bayti al-Maqdisi ilā ḥamli Ḍawʾi al-Makāni wa-tawṣīlihi ilā al-māristāni alladhī fī Dimashqi al-Shāmi fa-dhahaba bihi wa-alqāhu fī al-mustawqadi wa-dhahaba ilā ḥāli sabīlihi
sentences.l: And after that they turned to the third, and he was the camel-driver whom the people of the House of the Holy-place hired for the carrying of Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the conveying-of-him to the hospital which (is) in Damascus of Syria; and he went with him and threw him in the furnace-room and went to the state of his way.
sentences.i: After that they turned to the third. He was the camel-driver whom the people of Jerusalem had hired to carry Ḍawʾ al-Makān to the hospital in Damascus; but he had taken him off, cast him down in the stokehole of a bathhouse, and gone his way.
sentences.n: The shadda in الجمّال is the print's; jammāl, “camel-man”, one who hires out camels and drives them. iktarawhu ahlu Bayti al-Maqdis, “the people of Jerusalem hired him”: the verb carries its own plural ending (-ū) although its subject follows, where Classical Arabic would use the singular (iktarāhu); spoken Arabic agrees in full, and the print keeps it so. iktarā, “to hire”. ilā ḥaml, “for the carrying”. māristān, a Persian word, “hospital”. Dimashq al-Shām, “Damascus of Syria”, the city's usual full name. mustawqad, “place of kindling”, the furnace-room that heats a bathhouse, as the next sentences make plain. dhahaba ilā ḥāli sabīlihi, “went about his business”. Ḍawʾ al-Makān, Kān Mā Kān's father, was left there sick.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالُوا لَهُ أَخْبِرْنَا أَنْتَ بِخَبَرِكَ وَاصْدُقْ فِي حَدِيثِكَ فَحَكَى لَهُ جَمِيعَ مَا وَقَعَ لَهُ مَعَ السُّلْطَانِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ وَكَيْفَ حَمَلَهُ مِنْ بَيْتِ الْمَقْدِسِ وَهُوَ ضَعِيفٌ عَلَى أَنْ يُوصِلَهُ إِلَى الشَّامِ وَيَرْمِيَهُ فِى الْمَارَسْتَانِ وَكَيْفَ جَاءَ لَهُ أَهْلُ بَيْتِ الْمَقْدِسِ بِالدَّرَاهِمِ فَأَخَذَهَا وَهَرَبَ بَعْدَ أَنْ رَمَاهُ عَلَى الْمَزْبَلَةِ الَّتِي بِجَانِبِ مُسْتَوْقَدِ الْحَمَّامِ
sentences.tr: thumma qālū lahu akhbirnā anta bi-khabarika wa-uṣduq fī ḥadīthika fa-ḥakā lahu jamīʿa mā waqaʿa lahu maʿa al-sulṭāni Ḍawʾi al-Makāni wa-kayfa ḥamalahu min Bayti al-Maqdisi wa-huwa ḍaʿīfun ʿalā an yūṣilahu ilā al-Shāmi wa-yarmiyahu fī al-māristāni wa-kayfa jāʾa lahu ahlu Bayti al-Maqdisi bi-al-darāhimi fa-akhadhahā wa-haraba baʿda an ramāhu ʿalā al-mazbalati allatī bi-jānibi mustawqadi al-ḥammāmi
sentences.l: Then they said to him: Inform us, you, of your news, and be-truthful in your telling. And he told him all that befell him with the sultan Ḍawʾ al-Makān, and how he carried him from the House of the Holy-place, and he weak, on (terms) that he convey-him to Syria and throw-him in the hospital; and how the people of the House of the Holy-place came to him with the dirhams, and he took them and fled, after he threw him on the dung-heap which (is) beside the furnace-room of the bath.
sentences.i: Then they said to him, “Tell us your story, and tell it truly.” So he told him all that had passed between him and Sultan Ḍawʾ al-Makān: how he had carried him, sick, from Jerusalem, on the understanding that he would take him to Syria and leave him in the hospital; how the people of Jerusalem had brought him the money; and how he had taken it and fled, after throwing him on the dung-heap beside the furnace of the bathhouse.
sentences.n: fa-ḥakā lahu, “he told him”, in the singular, though “they” had asked: the teller has one hearer in mind, presumably Kān Mā Kān, who speaks next. ḍaʿīf, “weak”, here “sick”. ʿalā an, “on (the terms) that”. ramā, “to throw”, in spoken usage often just “to put, leave (somewhere)”. jāʾa lahu … bi-al-darāhim, “came to him with the money”: Classical says jāʾahu bi-; jāʾa li- is spoken usage. dirham, the silver coin, stands for money in general. mazbala, “rubbish heap, dung-heap”. The hamza in جاء is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَمَّ كَلَامُهُ أَخَذَ السُّلْطَانُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ السَّيْفَ وَضَرَبَهُ فَرَمَى عُنُقَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā tamma kalāmuhu akhadha al-sulṭānu Kāna Mā Kāna al-sayfa wa-ḍarabahu fa-ramā ʿunuqahu
sentences.l: And when his speech was complete, the sultan Kān Mā Kān took the sword and struck him, and threw-off his neck.
sentences.i: When he had finished speaking, Sultan Kān Mā Kān took the sword and struck him, and his head went flying.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي أَحْيَانِي حَتَّى جَازَيْتُ هَذَا الْخَائِنَ بِمَا فَعَلَ مَعَ أَبِي فَإِنَّنِي سَمِعْتُ هَذِهِ الْحِكَايَةَ بِعَيْنِهَا مِنْ وَالِدِي السُّلْطَانِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī aḥyānī ḥattā jāzaytu hādhā al-khāʾina bi-mā faʿala maʿa abī fa-innanī samiʿtu hādhihi al-ḥikāyata bi-ʿaynihā min wālidī al-sulṭāni Ḍawʾi al-Makāni
sentences.l: And he said: Praise (be) to God, who kept-me-alive until I requited this traitor for what he did with my father; for indeed I heard this tale, its-very-self, from my father, the sultan Ḍawʾ al-Makān.
sentences.i: And he said, “Praise be to God, who has let me live to repay this traitor for what he did to my father; for I heard this very story from my father, Sultan Ḍawʾ al-Makān.”
sentences.n: The print has جازبت, a misprint for جازيت, corrected here. jāzā bi-, “to requite someone for”. faʿala maʿa, “to do (something) to”, literally “with”, the usual spoken construction. bi-ʿaynihā, “in its very self”: “this very story”. The hamza in الخائن is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمُلُوكُ لِبَعْضِهِمْ مَا بَقِيَ عَلَيْنَا إِلَّا الْعَجُوزُ شَوَاهِي الْمُلَقَّبَةُ بِذَاتِ الدَّوَاهِي فَإِنَّهَا سَبَبُ هَذِهِ الْبَلَايَا حَيْثُ أَوْقَعَتْنَا فِى الرَّزَايَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-mulūku li-baʿḍihim mā baqiya ʿalaynā illā al-ʿajūzu Shawāhī al-mulaqqabatu bi-Dhāti al-Dawāhī fa-innahā sababu hādhihi al-balāyā ḥaythu awqaʿatnā fī al-razāyā
sentences.l: And the kings said to one-another: There remains not upon us except the old-woman Shawāhī, the one-surnamed Dhāt al-Dawāhī, for she (is) the cause of these afflictions, since she made-us-fall into the calamities.
sentences.i: Then the kings said to one another, “Only the old woman Shawāhī, called Dhāt al-Dawāhī, is left for us to deal with; for she is the cause of all these afflictions, since it was she who cast us into these calamities.”
sentences.n: qāla li-baʿḍihim, literally “said to some of them”, is the spoken way of saying “to one another” (Classical baʿḍuhum li-baʿḍ). mā baqiya ʿalaynā illā, “nothing remains upon us but”: the one task left. Rhyme: balāyā / razāyā, both “calamities”, chiming with her nickname Dhāt al-Dawāhī, “She of the Calamities”. ḥaythu, “where”, here “since, in that”.

sentences.t: وَمَنْ لَنَا بِهَا حَتَّى نَأْخُذَ مِنْهَا الثَّأْرَ وَنَكْشِفَ الْعَارَ
sentences.tr: wa-man lanā bihā ḥattā naʾkhudha minhā al-thaʾra wa-nakshifa al-ʿāra
sentences.l: And who (is) for us with her, that we may take from her the blood-revenge and uncover the shame?
sentences.i: But who will bring her within our reach, so that we may take our vengeance on her and lift this shame from us?
sentences.n: The print has ونكشت, a misprint for ونكشف, corrected here. man lanā bihā, “who is there for us with her?”: who will deliver her into our hands. kashafa al-ʿār, “to uncover (that is, remove) the disgrace”. Rhyme: thaʾr / ʿār.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ رُومْزَانُ عَمُّ الْمَلِكِ كَانَ مَا كَانَ لَابُدَّ مِنْ حُضُورِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku Rūmzānu ʿammu al-maliki Kāna Mā Kāna lā budda min ḥuḍūrihā
sentences.l: And King Rūmzān, paternal-uncle of King Kān Mā Kān, said to him: There is no escape from her coming.
sentences.i: King Rūmzān, the uncle of King Kān Mā Kān, said to him, “She must be made to come.”
sentences.n: lā budda min, “there is no avoiding”, the stock way of saying “must”; the print writes it as one word, لابد. “Her” is the old woman Shawāhī, on whom the kings mean to take revenge.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ رُومْزَانَ كَتَبَ كِتَابًا مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ وَأَرْسَلَهُ إِلَى جَدَّتِهِ الْعَجُوزِ شَوَاهِي الْمُلَقَّبَةِ بِذَاتِ الدَّوَاهِي وَذَكَرَ لَهَا فِيهِ أَنَّهُ غَلَبَ عَلَى مَمْلَكَةِ دِمَشْقَ وَالْمَوْصِلِ وَالْعِرَاقِ وَكَسَرَ عَسْكَرَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَأَسَرَ مُلُوكَهُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika Rūmzāna kataba kitāban min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi wa-arsalahu ilā jaddatihi al-ʿajūzi Shawāhī al-mulaqqabati bi-Dhāti al-Dawāhī wa-dhakara lahā fīhi annahu ghalaba ʿalā mamlakati Dimashqa wa-al-Mawṣili wa-al-ʿIrāqi wa-kasara ʿaskara al-muslimīna wa-asara mulūkahum
sentences.l: Then King Rūmzān wrote a letter from his time and his hour and sent it to his grandmother, the old-woman Shawāhī, the surnamed Dhāt al-Dawāhī, and mentioned to her in it that he had prevailed over the kingdom of Damascus and Mosul and Iraq, and broken the army of the Muslims and captured their kings.
sentences.i: Then King Rūmzān at once wrote a letter and sent it to his grandmother, the old woman Shawāhī, called Dhāt al-Dawāhī, Mistress of Calamities. In it he told her that he had conquered the kingdom of Damascus, Mosul and Iraq, routed the army of the Muslims and taken their kings captive.
sentences.n: min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi, “from his time and his hour”, at once. jadda is “grandmother”; Shawāhī is in fact the mother of his mother's father, so the word is used loosely. Every claim in the letter is a lie, the bait of the trap: Rūmzān has made peace with the Muslims and found that he is one of their royal house. kasara al-ʿaskar, “to break an army”, to rout it.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ أُرِيدُ أَنْ تَحْضُرِي عِنْدِي مِنْ كُلِّ بُدٍّ أَنْتِ وَالْمَلِكَةُ صَفِيَّةُ بِنْتُ الْمَلِكِ أَفْرِيدُونَ مَلِكِ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةِ وَمَنْ شِئْتُمْ مِنْ أَكَابِرِ النَّصَارَى مِنْ غَيْرِ عَسْكَرٍ فَإِنَّ الْبِلَادَ أَمَانٌ لِأَنَّهَا صَارَتْ تَحْتَ أَيْدِينَا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla urīdu an taḥḍurī ʿindī min kulli buddin anti wa-al-malikatu Ṣafiyyatu bintu al-maliki Afrīdūna maliki al-Qusṭanṭīniyyati wa-man shiʾtum min akābiri al-naṣārā min ghayri ʿaskarin fa-inna al-bilāda amānun li-annahā ṣārat taḥta aydīnā
sentences.l: And he said: I want that you come to me by every necessity, you and Queen Ṣafiyya, daughter of King Afrīdūn, king of Constantinople, and whom you-all wish of the great-ones of the Christians, without an army; for the lands are safety, because they have become under our hands.
sentences.i: He wrote, “I want you to come to me without fail, you and Queen Ṣafiyya, daughter of King Afrīdūn, king of Constantinople, and whichever of the Christian nobles you please, but without an army; for the country is safe, now that it is in our hands.”
sentences.n: min kulli buddin, “by every necessity”, without fail; the shadda on بدّ is the print's. naṣārā, “Christians”, literally “Nazarenes”. The country is “safety” (amān), a noun used for an adjective: the colloquial way of saying a place is safe. The ruse is to draw her in without her guards.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ الْكِتَابُ إِلَيْهَا وَقَرَأَتْهُ وَعَرَفَتْ خَطَّ الْمَلِكِ رُومْزَانَ فَرِحَتْ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَتَجَهَّزَتْ مِنْ وَقْتِهَا وَسَاعَتِهَا لِلسَّفَرِ هِيَ وَالْمَلِكَةُ صَفِيَّةُ أُمُّ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَمَنْ صَحِبَهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣala al-kitābu ilayhā wa-qaraʾathu wa-ʿarafat khaṭṭa al-maliki Rūmzāna fariḥat faraḥan shadīdan wa-tajahhazat min waqtihā wa-sāʿatihā li-al-safari hiya wa-al-malikatu Ṣafiyyatu ummu Nuzhati al-Zamāni wa-man ṣaḥibahum
sentences.l: And when the letter reached her and she read it and knew the hand of King Rūmzān, she rejoiced a severe rejoicing, and made-ready from her time and her hour for the journey, she and Queen Ṣafiyya, mother of Nuzhat al-Zamān, and whoever accompanied them.
sentences.i: When the letter reached her and she had read it and recognised King Rūmzān's hand, she was overjoyed, and at once made ready for the journey, she and Queen Ṣafiyya, the mother of Nuzhat al-Zamān, and all who went with them.
sentences.n: fariḥat faraḥan shadīdan, “she rejoiced a great rejoicing”: the verb strengthened by its own noun. khaṭṭ, “handwriting”. The hamza in قرأته is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا مُسَافِرِينَ حَتَّى وَصَلُوا إِلَى بَغْدَادَ فَتَقَدَّمَ الرَّسُولُ وَأَخْبَرَهُمْ بِحُضُورِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū musāfirīna ḥattā waṣalū ilā Baghdāda fa-taqaddama al-rasūlu wa-akhbarahum bi-ḥuḍūrihā
sentences.l: And they did not cease travelling until they reached Baghdad; and the messenger went-ahead and informed them of her coming.
sentences.i: They travelled on until they reached Baghdad, and the messenger went ahead and told the kings that she had come.
sentences.n: lam yazālū, “they did not cease”, with a participle: “they kept on travelling”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ رُومْزَانُ الْمَصْلَحَةُ تَقْتَضِي أَنَّنَا نَلْبَسُ لُبْسَ الْإِفْرِنْجِ وَنُقَابِلُ الْعَجُوزَ حَتَّى نَأْمَنَ مِنْ خِدَاعِهَا وَحِيَلِهَا فَقَالُوا سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Rūmzānu al-maṣlaḥatu taqtaḍī annanā nalbasu lubsa al-Ifranji wa-nuqābilu al-ʿajūza ḥattā naʾmana min khidāʿihā wa-ḥiyalihā fa-qālū samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: And Rūmzān said: The advantage requires that we wear the wear of the Franks and meet the old-woman, so that we may be-safe from her deceit and her tricks. And they said: Hearing and obedience.
sentences.i: Rūmzān said, “Prudence requires that we dress in Frankish clothes and so go out to meet the old woman, so that we may be safe from her deceit and her wiles.” They answered with hearing and obedience.
sentences.n: al-maṣlaḥa taqtaḍī, “the best course requires”. annanā nalbasu, “that we wear”, with the plain indicative after anna, as in speech; Classical would say an nalbasa. lubs, “wearing, clothes”, colloquial; the next sentence has the Classical libās. al-Ifranj, “the Franks”, the Europeans. The hamza in نأمن is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ لَبِسُوا لِبَاسَ الْإِفْرِنْجِ فَلَمَّا رَأَتْ ذَلِكَ قَضَى فَكَانَ قَالَتْ وَحَقِّ الرَّبِّ الْمَعْبُودِ لَوْلَا أَنِّي أَعْرِفُكُمْ لَقُلْتُ إِنَّكُمْ إِفْرِنْجٌ
sentences.tr: thumma innahum labisū libāsa al-Ifranji fa-lammā raʾat dhālika Qaḍā Fakāna qālat wa-ḥaqqi al-rabbi al-maʿbūdi law-lā annī aʿrifukum la-qultu innakum Ifranjun
sentences.l: Then they wore the clothing of the Franks; and when Qaḍā Fakān saw that, she said: By the right of the Lord, the worshipped, were-it-not that I know you, I would have said that you are Franks.
sentences.i: So they put on Frankish dress; and when Qaḍā Fakān saw it she said, “By the Lord who is worshipped, if I did not know you, I would say you were Franks!”
sentences.n: wa-ḥaqqi, “by the right (of)”, an oath formula. law-lā …, la-…, “were it not that …, then …”. The hamza in رأت is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ رُومْزَانَ تَقَدَّمَ أَمَامَهُمْ وَخَرَجُوا يُقَابِلُونَ الْعَجُوزَ فِى أَلْفِ فَارِسٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Rūmzāna taqaddama amāmahum wa-kharajū yuqābilūna al-ʿajūza fī alfi fārisin
sentences.l: Then Rūmzān went-forward in-front-of them, and they went out meeting the old-woman in a thousand horsemen.
sentences.i: Then Rūmzān rode at their head, and they went out with a thousand horsemen to meet the old woman.
sentences.n: kharajū yuqābilūna, “they went out, meeting”: the second verb gives the purpose. fī alf fāris, “in a thousand horsemen”, at the head of a thousand riders.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَقَعَتِ الْعَيْنُ فِى الْعَيْنِ تَرَجَّلَ رُومْزَانُ عَنْ جَوَادِهِ وَسَعَى إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waqaʿati al-ʿaynu fī al-ʿayni tarajjala Rūmzānu ʿan jawādihi wa-saʿā ilayhā
sentences.l: And when the eye fell on the eye, Rūmzān dismounted from his steed and hastened to her.
sentences.i: When they came face to face, Rūmzān dismounted from his horse and hurried towards her.
sentences.n: waqaʿati al-ʿaynu fī al-ʿayni, “the eye fell on the eye”, a stock phrase for two parties coming into sight of each other. tarajjala, “to dismount, go on foot” (rijl, “foot”); the shadda on ترجّل is the print's.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ وَعَرَفَتْهُ تَرَجَّلَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَعَانَقَتْهُ فَقَرَطَ بِيَدِهِ عَلَى أَضْلَاعِهَا حَتَّى كَادَ أَنْ يَقْصِفَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathu wa-ʿarafathu tarajjalat ilayhi wa-ʿānaqathu fa-qaraṭa bi-yadihi ʿalā aḍlāʿihā ḥattā kāda an yaqṣifahā
sentences.l: And when she saw him and knew him, she dismounted to him and embraced him; and he squeezed(?) with his hand upon her ribs until he almost snapped them.
sentences.i: When she saw him and knew him, she dismounted and embraced him; and he gripped her ribs with his hand until he all but broke them.
sentences.n: The verb فقرط is doubtful. qaraṭa is not a known verb for this; the sense from the rest of the sentence is “squeezed, crushed”, and the word may be a colloquial one (compare spoken qaraṣ, “to pinch”) or a corruption of the print. The vowels given are a guess. kāda an yaqṣifahā, “he was about to snap them”: the feminine -hā takes up aḍlāʿ, “ribs”, as broken plurals do. The hamza in رأته is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ مَا هَذَا يَا وَلَدِي فَلَمْ تُتِمَّ كَلَامَهَا حَتَّى نَزَلَ إِلَيْهِمَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَالْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat mā hādhā yā waladī fa-lam tutimma kalāmahā ḥattā nazala ilayhimā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-al-wazīru Dandānu
sentences.l: And she said: What is this, O my son? And she had not completed her speech until there came-down to the two-of-them Kān Mā Kān and the vizier Dandān.
sentences.i: “What is this, my son?” she said; but before she had finished speaking, Kān Mā Kān and the vizier Dandān had dismounted and come down on the two of them.
sentences.n: lam tutimma … ḥattā, “she had not finished … when”: the second action cuts into the first. nazala ilā, “to come down on”, here both dismounting and falling upon.

sentences.t: وَزَعَقَتِ الْفُرْسَانُ عَلَى مَنْ مَعَهَا مِنَ الْجَوَارِي وَالْغِلْمَانِ وَأَخَذُوهُمْ جَمِيعَهُمْ وَرَجَعُوا إِلَى بَغْدَادَ وَأَمَرَهُمْ رُومْزَانُ أَنْ يُزَيِّنُوا بَغْدَادَ فَزَيَّنُوهَا ثَلٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: wa-zaʿaqati al-fursānu ʿalā man maʿahā mina al-jawārī wa-al-ghilmāni wa-akhadhūhum jamīʿahum wa-rajaʿū ilā Baghdāda wa-amarahum Rūmzānu an yuzayyinū Baghdāda fa-zayyanūhā thalāthata ayyāmin
sentences.l: And the horsemen shouted upon whoever was with her of the slave-girls and the pages, and took them, all of them, and returned to Baghdad; and Rūmzān commanded them to adorn Baghdad, and they adorned it three days.
sentences.i: The horsemen fell with shouts on the slave-girls and pages who were with her and seized every one of them. Then they went back to Baghdad, and Rūmzān ordered the city to be decorated, and it was decorated for three days.
sentences.n: zaʿaqa ʿalā, “to shout at”, here to charge with a cry; zaʿaqa is a colloquial verb. jawārī, “slave-girls”; ghilmān, “pages, young male servants”. Decking the city out is the usual sign of public rejoicing. ثلٰثة is the print's spelling, with the long ā written as a small (dagger) alif.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخْرَجُوا بِالْعَجُوزِ شَوَاهِي الْمُلَقَّبَةِ بِذَاتِ الدَّوَاهِي وَعَلَى رَأْسِهَا طُرْطُورٌ أَحْمَرُ مِنَ الْخُوصِ مُكَلَّلٌ بِرَوْثِ الْحَمِيرِ وَقُدَّامَهَا مُنَادٍ يُنَادِي هَذَا جَزَاءُ مَنْ يَتَجَارَى عَلَى الْمُلُوكِ وَعَلَى أَوْلَادِ الْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: thumma akhrajū bi-al-ʿajūzi Shawāhī al-mulaqqabati bi-Dhāti al-Dawāhī wa-ʿalā raʾsihā ṭurṭūrun aḥmaru mina al-khūṣi mukallalun bi-rawthi al-ḥamīri wa-quddāmahā munādin yunādī hādhā jazāʾu man yatajārā ʿalā al-mulūki wa-ʿalā awlādi al-mulūki
sentences.l: Then they brought-out the old-woman Shawāhī, the surnamed Dhāt al-Dawāhī, and on her head a red tall-cap of palm-leaf crowned with the dung of the donkeys, and before her a crier crying: This is the reward of whoever dares against the kings and against the children of the kings!
sentences.i: Then they brought out the old woman Shawāhī, called Dhāt al-Dawāhī, wearing on her head a tall red cap of plaited palm-leaf garlanded with donkey dung, and before her went a crier calling out, “This is the reward of whoever presumes against kings and the children of kings!”
sentences.n: akhrajū bi-, “they brought out”, with a bi- that the causative verb does not need: the spoken language says ṭalaʿū bi- or kharajū bi-, and the two constructions have run together. The ṭurṭūr is a tall conical cap, the dunce's cap in which offenders were paraded through the streets; khūṣ is palm-leaf. يتجارى, yatajārā, stands for yatajarraʾu, “dares, presumes”: the hamza has been dropped and the verb reshaped, a common Middle Arabic softening. The hamza in رأسها is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَلَبُوهَا عَلَى بَابِ بَغْدَادَ وَلَمَّا رَأَى أَصْحَابُهَا مَا جَرَى لَهَا أَسْلَمُوا كُلُّهُمْ جَمِيعًا
sentences.tr: thumma ṣalabūhā ʿalā bābi Baghdāda wa-lammā raʾā aṣḥābuhā mā jarā lahā aslamū kulluhum jamīʿan
sentences.l: Then they crucified her upon the gate of Baghdad; and when her companions saw what had happened to her, they became-Muslims, all of them together.
sentences.i: Then they crucified her on the gate of Baghdad; and when her followers saw what had befallen her, every one of them embraced Islam.
sentences.n: ṣalaba, “to crucify, gibbet”: to hang up a body, alive or dead, for public display. aslama, “to submit”, to become a Muslim. kulluhum jamīʿan, “all of them altogether”, a doubled emphasis. The hamza in رأى is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَعَمَّهُ رُومْزَانَ وَنُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ وَالْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ تَعَجَّبُوا لِهَذِهِ السِّيرَةِ الْعَجِيبَةِ وَأَمَرُوا الْكُتَّابَ أَنْ يُؤَرِّخُوهَا فِى الْكُتُبِ حَتَّى تُقْرَأَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِمْ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Kāna Mā Kāna wa-ʿammahu Rūmzāna wa-Nuzhata al-Zamāni wa-al-wazīra Dandāna taʿajjabū li-hādhihi al-sīrati al-ʿajībati wa-amarū al-kuttāba an yuʾarrikhūhā fī al-kutubi ḥattā tuqraʾa min baʿdihim
sentences.l: Then Kān Mā Kān and his paternal-uncle Rūmzān and Nuzhat al-Zamān and the vizier Dandān marvelled at this wondrous life-story, and commanded the scribes that they record-it in the books, so that it be read after them.
sentences.i: Then Kān Mā Kān, his uncle Rūmzān, Nuzhat al-Zamān and the vizier Dandān marvelled at this wonderful history, and ordered the scribes to set it down in books, so that it might be read by those who came after them.
sentences.n: After inna the names stand in the accusative (ʿammahu, Nuzhata, al-wazīra); Kān Mā Kān, a phrase used as a name, does not change. sīra, “life-story, history”, the word used for the long popular romances of heroes. arrakha, “to date, chronicle”. The shadda on الكتّاب is the print's; the hamza in يؤرخوها and تقرأ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَقَامُوا بَقِيَّةَ الزَّمَانِ فِى الْعَيْشِ وَالْهَنَاهِ إِلَى أَنْ أَتَاهُمْ هَادِمُ اللَّذَّاتِ وَمُفَرِّقُ الْجَمَاعَاتِ
sentences.tr: wa-aqāmū baqiyyata al-zamāni fī al-ʿayshi wa-al-hanāʾati ilā an atāhum hādimu al-ladhdhāti wa-mufarriqu al-jamāʿāti
sentences.l: And they remained the rest of the time in the living and the well-being, until there came to them the Destroyer of the delights and the Sunderer of the companies.
sentences.i: And they lived out the rest of their days in comfort and contentment, until there came to them the Destroyer of Delights and the Sunderer of Companies.
sentences.n: The print has اللّعيش, a misprint for العيش, corrected here. ʿaysh, “living”, here the good life. والهناه is hanāʾa, “well-being, delight” (more often hanāʾ), written without its hamza and with ه for ة. The Destroyer of Delights and Sunderer of Companies is Death, in the rhymed formula (ladhdhāt / jamāʿāt) with which the tales of the Nights close.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا آخِرُ مَا انْتَهَى إِلَيْنَا مِنْ تَصَارِيفِ الزَّمَانِ بِالْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ وَوَلَدِهِ شَرْكَانَ وَوَلَدِهِ ضَوْ الْمَكَانِ وَوَلَدِ وَلَدِهِ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَبِنْتِهِ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَبِنْتِهَا قَضَى فَكَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā ākhiru mā intahā ilaynā min taṣārīfi al-zamāni bi-al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni wa-waladihi Sharrukāna wa-waladihi Ḍaw al-Makāni wa-waladi waladihi Kāna Mā Kāna wa-bintihi Nuzhati al-Zamāni wa-bintihā Qaḍā Fakāna
sentences.l: And this is the last of what has come-down to us of the turnings of the time with King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, and his son Sharrukān, and his son Ḍawʾ al-Makān, and the son of his son Kān Mā Kān, and his daughter Nuzhat al-Zamān, and her daughter Qaḍā Fakān.
sentences.i: And this is all that has come down to us of the turns of fortune that befell King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, his son Sharrukān, his son Ḍawʾ al-Makān, his grandson Kān Mā Kān, his daughter Nuzhat al-Zamān, and her daughter Qaḍā Fakān.
sentences.n: The tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, begun many nights ago, ends here, on a rhyme in -ān carried through the names: Nuʿmān, Makān, Kān, Zamān, Fakān. taṣārīf al-zamān, “the turnings of time”, the changes of fortune. The print spells the name ضو المكان, without the hamza of ḍawʾ, “light”; it is kept and read as written. Qaḍā Fakān is Nuzhat al-Zamān's daughter by Sharrukān, born before the two learned they were brother and sister. The hamza in آخر is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ قَالَ لِشَهْرَ زَادَ أَشْتَهِي أَنْ تَحْكِيَ لِي شَيْأً مِنْ حِكَايَةِ الطُّيُورِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika qāla li-Shahrazāda ashtahī an taḥkiya lī shayʾan min ḥikāyati al-ṭuyūri
sentences.l: Then the king said to Shahrazād: I desire that you tell me something of the tale of the birds.
sentences.i: Then the king said to Shahrazād, “I should like you to tell me something of the stories of birds.”
sentences.n: The frame breaks in: the king speaks between tales. The print sets the name in two words, شهر زاد; the spacing is kept. ishtahā, “to desire, crave”, in speech the ordinary word for “I'd like”. شيأ is the print's spelling of shayʾan, with the hamza on an alif.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا أُخْتُهَا لَمْ أَرَ الْمَلِكَ فِي طُولِ هَذِهِ الْمُدَّةِ انْشَرَحَ صَدْرُهُ غَيْرَ هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ وَأَرْجُو أَنْ تَكُونَ عَاقِبَتُكِ مَعَهُ مَحْمُودَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā ukhtuhā lam ara al-malika fī ṭūli hādhihi al-muddati insharaḥa ṣadruhu ghayra hādhihi al-laylati wa-arjū an takūna ʿāqibatuki maʿahu maḥmūdatan
sentences.l: And her sister said to her: I have not seen the king, in the length of this period, his breast expanded, except this night; and I hope that your outcome with him will be praiseworthy.
sentences.i: Her sister said to her, “In all this long time I have never seen the king so glad at heart as he is tonight; I hope your end with him will be a happy one.”
sentences.n: The sister is Dunyāzād, not named here. lam ara al-malika … insharaḥa ṣadruhu, “I have not seen the king (whose) breast expanded”: a second verb follows the object without a joining word, as in speech. inshiraḥ al-ṣadr, “the expanding of the breast”, is gladness. ʿāqiba, “outcome, end”: she hopes the nights will end in Shahrazād's life being spared.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ الْمَلِكُ أَدْرَكَهُ النَّوْمُ فَنَامَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna al-maliku adrakahu al-nawmu fa-nāma
sentences.l: And the king, sleep had overtaken him, and he slept.
sentences.i: And sleep had overtaken the king, and he slept.
sentences.n: kāna … adrakahu, “had overtaken him”: kāna with a past verb gives a pluperfect.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
